source: Zhang, Wang, Chen, Mansur, Sarhangian (2025) Comparing Exploration-Exploitation Strategies of LLMs and Humans: Insights from Standard Multi-armed Bandit Experiments
finding: Reasoning models and thinking budgets on a stationary 2-armed and a non-stationary 4-armed bandit, compared with human data. More thinking gave more directed exploration and less random exploration. In the stationary task thinking LLMs reached human levels. In the non-stationary task they did not.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-flash, DeepSeek-V3 and thinking versions o3-mini, Gemini-2.5-flash, DeepSeek-R1. Human data: 45 participants (stationary), 31 participants (non-stationary). o3-mini high-thinking: random exploration below the human level and directed exploration above it. Gemini-2.5-flash: raising the thinking budget moved directed exploration toward, but not past, the human level. Basic LLMs in the 4-armed task accumulated regret much faster than humans; thinking cut the regret to near human level in some scenarios.
quote: in more complex, non-stationary environments, LLMs struggle to match human adaptability, particularly in effective directed exploration
limits: Not the Krishnamurthy hard instance and not the suffix-failure metric. Choice-model fits and short horizons (20 trials in the stationary task). Thinking budget is a coarse knob (low/high, or budget 0 vs more).
agent_relevance: Closest direct data for gap 1: more thinking raises directed exploration in two models. The budget at which suffix failure vanishes was not measured on the Krishnamurthy metric.

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026, v4) Should You Use Your Large Language Model to Explore or Exploit?
finding: Splits exploit from explore. With raw (unsummarised) history, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 struggle on a simple exploit puzzle (name the arm with the highest empirical reward), which partly explains the Krishnamurthy and Nie failures. Reasoning models do much better.
numbers: GPT-5-mini reached perfect performance on the simple MAB exploit puzzle; accuracy rose from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 to GPT-5. 4 prompt designs (buttons or adverts, with or without CoT). On contextual-bandit puzzles, summaries and tool use helped on linear tasks, but every LLM stayed below plain linear regression, also on non-linear tasks (UAI 2026 version).
quote: reasoning models show the most promise for solving exploitation tasks, although they are still too expensive or too slow
limits: Tests exploitation only, not end-to-end exploration. Cost: one exploit call carries 5,000 to 8,000 prompt tokens, about 80 to 230 s per call; about 100 calls per experiment took 30 minutes to several hours.
agent_relevance: A reasoning model can read raw history and pick the best arm. The remaining weakness is deciding to explore, not arithmetic on the history. Use the model for exploit and a rule for explore.

source: Arumugam and Griffiths (ICLR 2026) Toward Efficient Exploration by Large Language Model Agents
finding: Instead of asking the LLM to behave like a bandit algorithm, separate LLM calls implement posterior sampling (PSRL): update the posterior, sample a hypothesis, act greedily on it. This scaffolded Thompson sampling beat prompt-only LLM agents. Swapping in a reasoning model (R1) helped baselines but did not beat the scaffold.
numbers: 5-armed Bernoulli bandit, horizon T=100: LLM-PSRL had a better cumulative regret curve than classic TS at sampling temperature 1.2. Customer-service bandit: K=20 periods. A Beta(1,1) prior written in language made the posterior LLM keep success and failure counts. R1 on combination lock (20 trials) and Wordle (40 trials): improvement for every agent, but not a statistically significant gain over LLM-PSRL running on weaker GPT-4o. RiverSwim: GPT-4o PSRL had near-linear regret; o1-mini PSRL matched classic PSRL.
quote: We find that R1 provides a performance improvement to all LLM agents
limits: Short horizons. Sampling temperature below 1 gave greedy-like behaviour. Several LLM calls per step (token cost not tabulated). Counting is done by the LLM, not a tool.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a prompt-written tally (Beta counts in words) works at T=100. Gap 1: the scaffold beat a raw reasoning model, so thinking tokens do not replace explicit allocation.

source: Schmied et al. (2025) LLMs are Greedy Agents: Effects of RL Fine-tuning on Decision-Making Abilities (try-all and exploration-bonus ablations)
finding: Gap 6 data. A try-all rule (play every arm once first, copied from UCB) gave the biggest regret gain of seven exploration mechanisms; a +1 bonus for untried arms during RL fine-tuning raised coverage 50% to 70%. Try-all was run with a rationale template during fine-tuning, so it is not a pure prompt test.
numbers: Gemma2 2B/9B/27B on 10-arm and 20-arm bandits. Without CoT only 25% of actions are covered; with CoT 40% (2B) and 65% (9B, 27B); at 20 arms the largest models cover 45%. Knowing-doing gap: 87% correct rationales, yet 64% greedy actions when the rationale was right (58% greedy vs 21% optimal in the UCB check). Try-all: Gemma2 27B almost closes the gap to UCB. RLFT raised 2B coverage by 12%.
quote: Gemma2 27B almost closes the gap to the optimal UCB agent.
limits: Fine-tuned Gemma, not frontier reasoning models. Try-all costs K pulls up front, which hurts when K is large relative to the budget. The bonus helped only in fine-tuning; no prompt-only bonus was tested.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 half way: forced try-all raises coverage and cuts regret in small open models. A prompt-only untried-option bonus on frontier models remains untested. Cheap rule for the scaffold: touch each candidate once before ranking.

source: Monea, Bosselut, Brantley, Artzi (COLM 2025) LLMs Are In-Context Bandit Reinforcement Learners
finding: Prompt-level exploration works: randomly choosing which past episodes to show in the prompt (Stochastic ICRL) gave exploration without raising temperature, stabilised learning, and allowed learning from negative signals. The naive version needed positive-reward episodes only.
numbers: Contextual bandit built from classification: Banking77 (77 labels), CLINC150 (150), NLU, TREC. Qwen2.5-7B improved from 6.2% zero-shot to 72.2% with Stochastic ICRL, with no gold labels and no weight updates. Qwen2.5 0.5B to 72B: gains grow with size; Spearman correlation of accuracy with time step was higher (more stable) for Stochastic than for Naive+ on Banking77, CLINC150, NLU. Naive ICRL dips suddenly before recovering.
quote: exploration is the key ingredient necessary for ICRL behavior in LLMs
limits: Contextual bandit with binary reward and many labels, not an arm-allocation task. Open models only. The authors name learning from negative episodes as unsolved.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 6 from the prompt side: randomised context is a working prompt-only exploration device. The scaffold could randomise which past attempts it shows when retrying.

source: Park, Zhang, Wang, Ozdaglar, Zhang (2025, v5) Do LLM Agents Have Regret? A Case Study in Online Learning and Games
finding: Re-read for gap 7. GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo reach low regret on the canonical follow-the-leader counterexample and on the switch-at-c sequence when given raw history. They fail on a noisy alternating loss and on an adaptive loss. For the switch sequence, summarised history did far worse than raw history, which contradicts the idea that summaries are always better.
numbers: Raw vs summarised history regret on Example 2 (T=500): one-sided t-test p = 1.2e-157. Failure cases: noisy alternating loss and adaptive loss, GPT-4 trend statistic 1.0 and GPT-4 Turbo 0.97 or 1.0 (linear regret not rejected), against sublinear regret for a transformer trained with the proposed regret-loss. Settings are full-information online learning and bandit feedback, not Krishnamurthy-style hard instances.
limits: Failures are on designed sequences, one with an adversary that reacts to the agent. The text shows no prompt-only fix. The fix offered is training (regret-loss), not scaffolding.
agent_relevance: Refines K14 and K15: the set of tests where the LLM wins and loses is narrow. A flip that follows a simple pattern is spotted; a noisy or reactive flip is not. A scaffold should show raw recent history and an explicit changed-payoff check, not only cumulative means.

source: Taberner-Miller (2026) ParetoBandit: Budget-Paced Adaptive Routing for Non-Stationary LLM Serving
finding: Scaffold-side fix for non-stationary arms: a cost-aware contextual bandit with geometric forgetting on per-arm sufficient statistics, so old data decays and the router tracks silent changes in model quality or price. Uses a UCB rule, not a Gittins or Whittle index.
numbers: 1,824 benchmark prompts, three-model portfolio. Budget held within 0.4% of the ceiling. Up to +0.071 quality lift after a price or quality shift. A newly added model was integrated within 142 steps.
limits: Routing of requests across models, not allocation inside one reasoning trace. Quality scores come from benchmark labels. No LLM acts as the allocator.
agent_relevance: A gap 7 fix exists in bandit form: forgetting (discounted statistics) lets an allocator drop a plan that stopped working. The agent version is a decayed tally of recent attempts per plan, kept by a tool or written by the model.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: Linear probes on hidden states predict whether an intermediate answer is correct and also the correctness of the answer still to come, before it is written. Used for early exit.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-32B probe: ROC-AUC above 0.9 on AIME. Look-ahead probe on R1-Distill-Llama-8B, MATH: peak accuracy 79%; at 10%, 50% and 95% of the way through a chunk it is lower by 14, 10 and 5 points. Calibration error lowest (0.03) near the 60% position. Early exit at probe threshold 0.85: accuracy 88.2%, same as no early exit, tokens cut about 24%; threshold 0.9: 88.6% accuracy, 19% fewer tokens; up to +5 points over static early exit at equal token saving.
quote: models' hidden states encode correctness of future answers
limits: Open-weight models with white-box hidden states, so not usable by an API agent. Probes are trained per dataset; math probes beat logic probes. Accuracy at the earliest point is far from perfect. No rank correlation reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 for white-box models: partial reasoning carries a usable but weak signal early (about 65% accuracy at 10% of a chunk) and a good one near the end. For a prompt-only agent this does not transfer.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Sampling-Efficient Test-Time Scaling: Self-Estimating the Best-of-N Sampling in Early Decoding (ST-BoN)
finding: Without any reward model, samples whose early hidden states disagree with the others are cut and the most consistent one is kept. A monotonicity argument (early consistency raises the lower bound on final consistency) is given and tested.
numbers: Same accuracy as full Best-of-N at 70% to 80% less compute; at equal cost +3 to +4 accuracy points; dynamic GPU memory down over 80%, latency down about 50%.
limits: Needs hidden states (white-box). The theory assumes local Lipschitz continuity of next-token distributions. Not tested on weak-signal hard sets.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a no-verifier prune-early-then-continue scheme (one-round halving) beats full BoN at equal cost. It is the closest published relative of successive halving without a verifier. Multi-round halving over plans at equal total tokens is still untested.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Token confidence in a sliding group is used to stop low-confidence reasoning traces early (online) or to weight votes (offline). Large token savings; one documented failure from overconfident wrong traces.
numbers: AIME 2025, GPT-OSS-120B: pass@1 91.8%, majority vote at 512 samples 97.0%, DeepConf@512 99.9%; tokens down up to 84.7% in online mode. DeepConf-low saves 43% to 79% of tokens versus majority voting at 512 samples; it matches or gains in most cells (DeepSeek-8B AIME24 +5.8) but loses in a few (Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9). Aggressive top-10% filtering hurt GPT-OSS-120B (HMMT25 92.9 to 88.9 in one table column). DeepConf-high saves 18% to 59% with near-identical accuracy.
quote: it can sometimes hurt performance due to model overconfidence on incorrect problems
limits: Needs token log-probabilities. Models: DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3-8B/32B, GPT-OSS-20B/120B.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3, 5 and 9 together: early cutting on confidence works on average and fails where the model is confidently wrong. Keep the cut conservative.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Efficiently Scaling LLM Reasoning with Certaindex (Dynasor)
finding: Answer stabilisation: intermediate answers often stop changing long before the reasoning ends. A running stability score (Certaindex) allows early exit and shifts token budget from easy to hard queries.
numbers: Up to 50% compute saved with no accuracy drop and up to 3.3x higher throughput in serving. Token use cut 11% to 29% at the same accuracy; for the top 10% of problems, savings of 34% on AIME and 53% on MATH500. R1 emits about 3x more tokens than it needs (their Figure 2). In one MATH serving workload only about 10% of tokens were saved.
limits: Savings differ a lot by workload. Needs periodic probing of the model for its current answer.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a cheap black-box signal (does the current answer change when probed?) predicts when to stop. Probing for the current answer can be done in a scaffold.

source: Manvi, Singh, Ermon (2024) Adaptive Inference-Time Compute: LLMs Can Predict if They Can Do Better, Even Mid-Generation
finding: A fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B predicts mid-generation whether restarting would give a better answer, using one extra token. Used to decide how many samples to draw and to prune early.
numbers: Adaptive sampling: 1.2 samples on average capture 74% of the gain of 16 samples; 1.9 capture 84%. Early pruning stops 75% of unpromising samples from being fully generated and saves 56% of tokens with minimal loss. GSM8K 84% to 91% with 16 samples; AlpacaEval win rate against GPT-4 21% to 34%.
limits: Needs fine-tuning on LMSYS prompts; the self-prediction is trained, not prompted. 8B model.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 5: a model trained to report its chance of beating its current draft does so well enough to prune. The prompted, untrained version is the open question.

source: Xiong et al. (ICLR 2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
finding: Gap 5. Verbalised confidence from black-box LLMs is overconfident. Better prompts, sampling consistency and aggregation reduce it, but no method wins everywhere, and all fail on hard professional-knowledge tasks.
numbers: Verbalised values mostly fall in the 80% to 100% range, often in multiples of 5. Five LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 Chat, five dataset types. White-box methods beat black-box ones only narrowly (AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605). Failure prediction improves with scale but is far from ideal.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns of expressing confidence.
limits: Older models (2023). Confidence about an answer, not about a plan not yet tried.
agent_relevance: An allocator that trusts a self-stated success probability inherits this overconfidence: all options look good and spreading collapses. Prefer observed counts from real attempts over stated priors.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Gap 5 update. Reasoning models with long chains of thought are better calibrated than non-reasoning counterparts, and calibration improves as the chain unfolds.
numbers: Six reasoning models, six datasets: strictly better calibration in 33 of 36 settings. Removing slow-thinking behaviours (exploring, backtracking) lowers calibration. Non-reasoning models improve when guided to slow-think in context. Non-reasoning models still pile into the 95% bin and can show inflated AUROC with worse Brier score.
quote: reasoning models become increasingly better calibrated as their CoT unfolds
limits: Calibration of the answer after reasoning, not a per-option success estimate before any attempt. Some non-reasoning models beat reasoning ones in AUROC on some sets.
agent_relevance: Part-closes gap 5: newer reasoning models give more honest probabilities and honesty improves with thinking. Still untested as a per-plan success prior.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions, and a model can be trained to predict P(IK), the chance it knows the answer, before any answer is proposed. P(IK) calibration is weaker on new tasks.
numbers: P(IK) predictions are good and partly generalise across tasks; calibration worsens out of distribution; RLHF policy miscalibration is fixable with temperature tuning.
limits: 2022 models and a trained P(IK) head rather than a prompt. Format-sensitive: replacing an option with 'None of the above' harms calibration.
agent_relevance: Origin of the per-problem success estimate that adaptive allocators need (gap 5). Evidence that the estimate can be learned, with a loss under distribution shift.

source: Damani, Shenfeld, Peng, Bobu, Andreas (2024) Learning How Hard to Think (re-read for calibration)
finding: The allocator's difficulty predictor is a probe on hidden states trained on reward-model scores, not the LLM's own stated estimate. It is well calibrated on the sets studied. A failure mode is named: a problem with true success 0% predicted at 1% looks attractive and attracts a large budget.
numbers: Compute saved up to 50% at equal quality (Code), or quality up to +10% at fixed budget; 50% of coding problems have zero success probability (5% for Math). Predictor accuracy for routing 72% to 84% by task.
quote: if a problem has a true success rate of 0%, but its success rate is predicted to be 1%, it becomes an attractive candidate
limits: An offline variant avoids the near-zero pathology. Chat tasks gain only about 10% in compute.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to what overconfidence does: it hands budget to hopeless options. A per-option spend cap protects against it.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), Table 1 re-read for hard problems
finding: Gap 9. A window rule (stop when all answers in a window agree) saves far fewer samples on hard MATH than on easy sets, with little accuracy loss.
numbers: Average sample reduction: MATH -33.8% (window 8, max 64 samples), GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. GPT-3.5 on MATH: ESC accuracy 59.98 vs SC 60.32 (-0.34).
limits: Table 1 text extraction is garbled, so only the headline figures and the GPT-3.5 MATH row are used. Smaller windows save more but risk errors.
agent_relevance: Stop rules gain little when agreement is rare. On the hardest items they run to the cap, so a scaffold needs a separate give-up rule.

source: Li, Jamieson, DeSalvo, Rostamizadeh, Talwalkar (2018) Hyperband (JMLR), SVHN benchmark text
finding: Gap 3 failure case. On SVHN Hyperband finds a good configuration faster than random search, but Bayesian optimisation is competitive and SMAC with early stopping beats it. Early cutting is not uniformly best.
numbers: Three benchmarks. Hyperband over 20x faster than random search; SMAC (early) about 7x faster; the first Hyperband result at budget 5R is often competitive with other searchers at 50R. The most exploratory bracket s=4 vastly outperformed all methods on CIFAR-10 and MRBI and was nearly tied with SMAC (early) for first on SVHN. Infinite-horizon Hyperband did worse than finite horizon within 50R.
limits: Neural-network hyperparameters with fairly smooth loss curves. Not LLM reasoning. No rank-correlation figure in the passages read.
agent_relevance: Early cutting assumes rank at small budget predicts final rank. Where that is weak, repeat the most exploratory bracket (start many options, cut little).

source: Tang et al. (2024) Code Repair with LLMs gives an Exploration-Exploitation Tradeoff (REx)
finding: Iterative code refinement framed as an arm-acquiring bandit solved by Thompson sampling over programs; each refinement is a pull. It searches broadly but refines deeply on promising programs.
numbers: 1.5x to 5x fewer LLM calls (about 2x on APPS-Competition, 2-5x on loop invariants, 1.1-1.6x on ARC) with equal or more problems solved. Nonlinear loop invariants 73.7% vs 60.5% for a specialised solver. No speed-up on APPS Introductory.
limits: Needs test cases as a verifier (pass rate is the reward). Gains vanish on easy problems.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 side: bandit allocation over candidate programs works when a verifier exists. It says nothing about the weak-verifier case.

source: Search of arXiv titles and abstracts for LLM use of Gittins or Whittle indices (negative search)
finding: Gap 4. Searches on arXiv found no paper that measures an LLM computing or using a Gittins or Whittle index.
numbers: Queries 'LLM Whittle index' and 'Whittle language models restless' returned zero results. 'Gittins language model' returned two unrelated papers (agent-workflow model recommendation, 2610.26676; LLM-application serving, 2506.14851). 'non-stationary bandit LLM' returned UCB-style or Thompson-style papers only (for example ParetoBandit).
limits: Search covers only arXiv titles and abstracts; the general web search was unavailable (quota used up). A paper using the index without naming it, or a venue outside arXiv, would be missed.
agent_relevance: Treat the Gittins or Whittle index as untested for LLM agents. Use it only as a design rule (compute a per-option index outside the model) and test it.
